entry.title: Motion and the balance of forces

encoded.from: the published entry; no new reading

entry.coverage: One text per region, on the principles of motion. Not yet read: pendulum, inclined plane, projectiles, central forces, the machines; Biwald pp. 95-162 in detail; Erxleben §§49-78; Nollet on collision and the machines; the rest of Ferguson's Lectures II and III.

revised.change: British text changed from the Britannica (fails R1 clause 2) to Ferguson, Lectures on Select Subjects, 5th ed. 1776, read from the page images; the Britannica kept as supplementary

B.parts: Part I sections II-III, pp. 95-162; Part II art. IV from p. 185 and art. VIII pp. 271-286; preface to the 2nd ed.

N.parts: t. 1, Lesson III from p. 177; Lesson IV from p. 259

F.parts: Lecture I, Of matter and its properties, pp. 1-18; Lecture II, Of central forces, from p. 19; Lecture III, Of the mechanical powers, from p. 47; one passage of the lecture on hydrostatics, p. 106

EB.parts: Mechanics, vol. 3 from p. 32; entry Inertia, vol. 2 p. 840
EB.note: Fails R1 clause 2. Its treatise Mechanics reprints Ferguson's Lectures I-III nearly word for word (see texts.json), so claims from Mechanics are Ferguson's words. The entry Inertia is the Britannica's own.

placement.where: Twice: in Part I with the plain rules of motion, balance, collision and machines; in Part II, on forces between points, for contact and inertia
Third section, after bodies in general and before gravity
Lessons III and IV, with experiments on hanging balls

Inactivity among the properties of matter in Lecture I; the laws of motion at the head of Lecture II, on central forces; the quantity of motion as 'the foundation of all mechanics' at the head of Lecture III, on the mechanical powers
Inside the treatise Mechanics, with the properties of matter and central forces (Ferguson's Lectures I-III, reprinted)

claims.question: motion-quantity
claims.statement: Motions are as the products of masses into velocities, and forces compare the same way, being proportional to their effects.

reasons.detail: forces are proportional to their effects

claims.question: motion-quantity
claims.statement: From the beginning of the world the quantity of motion was reckoned as mass times velocity; the momentum of balanced forces is the absolute force times the initial velocity.

reasons.detail: reckoned so from the beginning of the world

claims.question: motion-quantity
claims.statement: The momentum of a moving body is its quantity of matter multiplied by its velocity.

quote.orig: the whole momentum or quantity of force of a moving body is the result of its quantity of matter multiplied by the velocity with which it is moved.

claims.question: motion-quantity
claims.statement: Nollet says the force of a moving body had always been thought to be its mass times its velocity.

claims.question: balance
claims.statement: Two bodies on a rigid rod over a fulcrum balance when, if they moved, their quantities of motion would be equal.

claims.question: balance
claims.statement: In any machine the excess of weight in one body is made up by the excess of velocity in the other; on this the whole of mechanics depends.

confidence.printed: Upon this easy principle depends the whole of mechanics

claims.question: balance
claims.statement: Erxleben's treatment of the machines has not been read.

claims.question: balance
claims.statement: Nollet's lessons on the machines have not been read.

claims.question: action-reaction
claims.statement: Reaction is always equal to the action that occasioned it; to doubt it is to misconceive it.

confidence.translation: must necessarily form a most incorrect idea of it
confidence.note: German wording to be copied from the page

quote.tr: Whoever can doubt that this reaction is always equal to the action that occasioned it must necessarily form a most incorrect idea of it.
quote.note: German original not reproduced in the entry

claims.question: action-reaction
claims.statement: Biwald deduces the equality of action and reaction from the mutual action of the points of matter, and notes that Boscovich derives the laws of collision from it.

reasons.detail: mutual action of points of matter

claims.question: action-reaction
claims.statement: In the hanging-ball experiments the ball at rest takes part of the striker's motion, and the striker loses what the other gains.

reasons.detail: hanging balls of ivory and lead

claims.question: action-reaction
claims.statement: The entry Inertia has bodies resist as much as they are resisted.

claims.question: collision
claims.statement: Hard or soft bodies move on together after the blow; elastic bodies spring apart.

claims.question: collision
claims.statement: Same rules of collision for hard, soft and elastic bodies.

claims.question: collision
claims.statement: Same rules of collision, shown on hanging balls.

claims.question: collision
claims.statement: The entry Collision refers to Mechanics, where the parts read do not treat it.

claims.question: hard-bodies
claims.statement: Nature has no perfectly hard bodies, so experiment can only approach the rules; but whether the law of continuity rightly proves this is still a question.

quote.orig: Bey harten Körpern hingegen geschieht der Uebergang der Bewegung in Ruhe plötzlich: deswegen haben einige aus dem Gesetze der Stetigkeit gefolgert, es könne keine völlig harten Körper geben. Dies lehrt nun zwar die Erfahrung, aber es ist noch die Frage, ob das Gesetz der Stetigkeit hier recht angebracht wird?
quote.tr: In hard bodies, on the other hand, the passage of motion into rest happens suddenly: for this reason some have concluded from the law of continuity that there can be no perfectly hard bodies. Experience indeed teaches this, but it is still the question whether the law of continuity is rightly applied here.

claims.question: hard-bodies
claims.statement: There is no perfectly hard matter: every blow leaves a dent at the place of contact.

claims.question: hard-bodies
claims.statement: No statement of Biwald's on perfectly hard bodies was located in the parts read; his denial of contact (pp. 196-197) bears on it.

claims.question: hard-bodies
claims.statement: Not found in the parts of the Mechanics read.

claims.question: inertia-force
claims.statement: A body at rest makes a real resistance to being moved, proportional to its quantity of matter; it is neither the air nor weight, since it acts in a vacuum and in every direction.

reasons.detail: a struck hanging ball; a heavier ball carried less far

quote.orig: Un corps en repos fait donc une résistance réelle à l'effort qui tend à le mouvoir. […] Il y a donc quelque chose de plus à vaincre, qu'une seule privation de mouvement.
quote.tr: A body at rest therefore makes a real resistance to the effort that tends to move it. […] There is therefore something more to overcome than a mere privation of motion.

claims.question: inertia-force
claims.statement: Inactivity or passiveness is the second property of matter, by which it endeavours to continue in its state of rest or motion.

quote.orig: inactivity, or passiveness … by which it always endeavours to continue in the state that it is in, whether of rest or motion

claims.question: inertia-force
claims.statement: The entry Inertia gives Newton's two definitions side by side without remark: a passive principle, and a power implanted in all matter that resists change.

quote.orig: a passive principle by which bodies persist in their motion or rest … a power implanted in all matter, whereby it resists any change endeavoured to be made in its state.

claims.question: inertia-force
claims.statement: Inertia is not a force of its own: it says only that something must set a body moving and something must stop it, which is the principle of sufficient reason applied to bodies.

quote.tr: So inertia is in fact nothing other than the principle of sufficient reason applied to the changes of state of bodies.
quote.note: German original not reproduced in the entry

claims.question: inertia-force
claims.statement: Erxleben reports that inertia has been taken for a force peculiar to bodies and questions whether a force that only resists, and has no size of its own, can be conceived.

confidence.printed: Läßt sich wohl eine Kraft gedenken
confidence.translation: Can one well conceive a force

reasons.detail: a force that never acts of itself is inconceivable

quote.orig: Aber braucht denn ein Ding eine eigne Kraft um das zu bleiben, was es ein Mahl ist? Läßt sich wohl eine Kraft gedenken, die niemahls von selbst wirkt sondern nur widersteht? die gar keine Grösse für sich hat, sondern nur groß oder klein ist, nachdem das ist, dem sie sich widersetzt?
quote.tr: But does a thing then need a force of its own to remain what it once is? Can one well conceive a force that never acts of itself but only resists? That has no size of its own, but is great or small according to what it resists?

claims.question: inertia-force
claims.statement: Bodies do not positively resist a change of state: they have a motive force, a continual striving to change place, and an opposite striving to keep place cannot be in the same substance. What mechanics calls resistance is the mutual action of bodies.

reasons.detail: two opposed strivings cannot be in one substance; the motive force is taught by the metaphysicians

persons.name: Roger Joseph Boscovich SJ
persons.note: Boscovich gave inertia to his points

quote.orig: Datur enim in corporibus vis motrix, quae, veluti metaphysici docent, consistit in continuo nisu, sive conatu mutandi locum. Quod si vero corpora mutationi status positive resisterent, daretur in iis quoque nisus, sive conatus conservandi loci; qui conatus tanquam sibi omnino oppositi eidem substantiae inesse non possunt.
quote.tr: For there is in bodies a motive force, which, as the metaphysicians teach, consists in a continual striving or endeavour to change place. But if bodies positively resisted a change of state, there would also be in them a striving or endeavour to keep their place; and these endeavours, being wholly opposed to each other, cannot be in the same substance.

claims.question: inertia-force
claims.statement: In the preface to the second edition Biwald keeps his view against critics who had sworn by Boscovich's words, and says the quarrel concerns the essence of body, not a word.

quote.orig: Illud enim illico adverti, Authores hos, cum Boscovichii theoriam exponendam sibi sumpsissent, ita in Authoris huius verba iurasse, ut ne latum quidem unguem ab eo recedendum esse existimarent. […] Neque de verbo ea lis versatur, sed eam, quam de corporis essentia tenemus, sententiam plane ingreditur.
quote.tr: For I noticed at once that these authors, having undertaken to expound Boscovich's theory, had so sworn by the words of this author that they thought they should not depart from him by a nail's breadth. […] Nor is this a quarrel about a word; it goes straight to the heart of the opinion we hold about the essence of body.

claims.question: motion-persistence
claims.statement: Matter always endeavours to continue in the state it is in, whether of rest or motion.

claims.question: motion-persistence
claims.statement: Something must set a body moving and something must stop it; without a cause its state does not change.

claims.question: first-law-grounds
claims.statement: Erxleben grounds inertia on the principle of sufficient reason.

claims.question: first-law-grounds
claims.statement: The first law can be proved neither from the nature of bodies nor from the phenomena, since nothing in nature is ever absolutely at rest or moves uniformly in a straight line.

reasons.detail: no absolute rest or uniform straight motion in nature

claims.question: first-law-grounds
claims.statement: Against Euler: we do not know the inner natures of things; by the same reasoning a lone body could circle any point; and a priori, accelerated motion on some curve is infinitely more probable than rest or uniform straight motion.

reasons.detail: the argument proves too much; infinitely more curved states than straight ones

claims.question: motion-transfer
claims.statement: Collision is a matter of contact; since no matter is perfectly hard, a dent is always made at the place of contact.

quote.tr: a dent is always made at the place of contact
quote.note: French original not reproduced in the entry

claims.question: motion-transfer
claims.statement: How motion is communicated remains an unsearchable mystery for us, who do not know bodies' inner constitution; the expression is justified only in that one body acts on the other with a force depending on its motion.

quote.orig: Aber wie eigentlich diese Mittheilung der Bewegung (communicatio motus) geschieht, das bleibt wohl im Grunde für uns, die wir die Körper ihrer innern Beschaffenheit nach nicht kennen, ein unerforschliches Geheimniß; denn was geht bey der Mittheilung der Bewegung aus dem bewegten Körper in den durch ihn in Bewegung gesetzten über?
quote.tr: But how this communication of motion properly comes about remains at bottom, for us who do not know bodies in their inner constitution, an unsearchable mystery; for what passes, in the communication of motion, out of the moving body into the one set in motion by it?

claims.question: motion-transfer
claims.statement: There is no mathematical contact of bodies, only apparent contact; a repulsive force growing without limit as distance shrinks stops bodies short and changes their speeds by degrees.

reasons.detail: Boscovich's law of continuity: speed cannot jump from six degrees to three

quote.orig: Nullus igitur est corporum contactus mathematicus, seu stricte talis, qui tum habetur, cum duo corpora ita contigua sunt, ut inter ea non modo nihil interponatur, sed ne quidem interponi possit. Erit tamen contactus physicus, sive apparens, consistens in eo, quod duo corpora ita sint propinqua, ut inter ea nihil interponi posse videatur, quamvis reipsa intercedere quidpiam possit.
quote.tr: There is therefore no mathematical contact of bodies, or contact strictly so called, which there would be when two bodies are so adjacent that nothing not only is placed between them, but nothing could be. There will, however, be physical or apparent contact, consisting in two bodies being so near that it seems nothing could be placed between them, though in fact something may come between.

claims.question: motion-transfer
claims.statement: The parts of the Mechanics read do not take the question up.

claims.question: action-at-distance
claims.statement: Since bodies never touch, all their action on one another, collision included, is by forces across small distances.

claims.question: force-measure
claims.statement: Biwald sets out the quarrel (Leibniz and some Dutch, Italians and Germans for mass times velocity squared in actual motion; the English and French for the old measure) and sides with those who reduce it to a question of a name, given the number of demonstrations on each side.

quote.orig: complures rem ad quaestionem de nomine reducere conabantur, quibus ut assentiamur, facit demonstrationum numerus bene magnus, quas utraque pars pro sententiae suae veritate asserenda producit.
quote.tr: Several tried to reduce the matter to a question of a name; and what makes us agree with them is the very great number of demonstrations that each side produces for the truth of its own opinion.

claims.question: force-measure
claims.statement: Most were revolted by the new doctrine; both sides agree on the effects and differ only on why, so the affair, if not a question of a name, matters less to mechanics than it seemed; in practice force may be estimated by mass and simple velocity.

reasons.detail: agreement on the effects once time is considered

quote.orig: Et il faut avouer que si l'on fait entrer la considération du tems dans l'examen des faits qu'on apporte en preuves des forces vives, on se retrouve alors dans la route ordinaire […] Il suit de cet aveu & de sa restriction, que si l'affaire des forces vives n'est point une question de nom, au moins on peut dire qu'elle n'est pas d'une aussi grande conséquence qu'elle paroissoit devoir l'être pour la méchanique
quote.tr: And it must be admitted that if one brings the consideration of time into the examination of the facts offered as proofs of living forces, one finds oneself back on the ordinary road. […] It follows from this admission and its restriction that if the affair of living forces is not a question of a name, at least one can say it is not of so great consequence as it seemed it must be for mechanics.

claims.question: force-measure
claims.statement: Erxleben passes over the Leibnizian distinction of living and dead forces and the dispute over the measure of forces as too long for an elementary course.

claims.question: force-measure
claims.statement: The Britannica gives mass times velocity as the foundation of mechanics and does not mention the dispute.

confidence.printed: Upon this easy principle depends the whole of mechanics

claims.question: absolute-rest
claims.statement: If the earth turns and goes round the sun, as is very probable, no body on it is at rest except relative to other earthly things.

confidence.note: French wording to be copied from the page

claims.question: absolute-rest
claims.statement: Absolute rest exists nowhere in nature: forces depending on distance, internal motions, effluvia and heat keep every part of every body moving.

claims.question: inertia-weight
claims.statement: Erxleben rejects the view of Andreas Gordon that inertia and weight are the same, and also Euler's, who seems to him to make inertia the same as impenetrability.

claims.question: inertia-weight
claims.statement: The objection is specious: weight acts only downward, the resistance in every direction, and a long thread takes away a hanging ball's weight but not its resistance.

claims.question: inertia-moves
claims.statement: Some natural philosophers say inertia can itself give a body motion and offer experiments; Erxleben promises to show in his lectures that the experiments prove nothing of the kind.

claims.question: motion-quantity
claims.statement: The whole momentum or quantity of force of a moving body is its quantity of matter multiplied by its velocity; a body of 40 pounds at two miles a minute and one of 4 pounds at twenty would strike any obstacle with equal forces.

quote.orig: the whole momentum or quantity of force of a moving body is the result of its quantity of matter multiplied by the velocity with which it is moved.

claims.question: balance
claims.statement: Two bodies on any machine balance when the ascent of one multiplied into its weight equals the descent of the other multiplied into its weight; the excess of weight in one is made up by the excess of velocity in the other.

confidence.printed: Upon this easy principle depends the whole of mechanics: and it holds universally true

quote.orig: Upon this easy principle depends the whole of mechanics

claims.question: action-reaction
claims.statement: Ferguson does not state the law among the laws of motion in the parts read, but uses it as a known principle in hydrostatics: action and reaction are equal and contrary to each other.

quote.orig: since action and reaction are equal and contrary to each other

claims.question: collision
claims.statement: Ferguson's course has no section on the collision of bodies (Lectures I-III read; a search of the machine-read text of the whole book finds none).

claims.question: hard-bodies
claims.statement: Not taken up; a 'perfectly hard' bowl appears only in a thought experiment on friction.

claims.question: inertia-force
claims.statement: Inactivity or passiveness is the second property of matter, by which it always endeavours to continue in its state of rest or motion; twice the matter has twice the inactivity and needs twice the force to move or stop it. Force must be applied to overcome its 'inactivity or resistance', but no force of inertia is named.

reasons.detail: a stone never moves itself, as all men allow

quote.orig: inactivity, or passiveness; by which it always endeavours to continue in the state that it is in, whether of rest or motion.

claims.question: motion-persistence
claims.statement: A body once impelled goes on in that direction for ever with the same velocity, for of itself it could never swerve from a right line nor stop its course; when a body falls from motion to rest, some other body or cause stopped it.

quote.orig: for, of itself, it could never swerve from a right line, nor stop its course.

claims.question: first-law-grounds
claims.statement: That matter cannot move itself is allowed by all men; that it does not tend to rest is shown by taking away what stops it: a bowl on a green stops by friction and the air, would go farther on polished glass, and with no air would go round the earth for ever.

reasons.detail: the bowl on a green made ever smoother, then without air

claims.question: motion-transfer
claims.statement: Not taken up in the parts read.

claims.question: force-measure
claims.statement: Ferguson measures the force with which a body strikes an obstacle by its quantity of matter times its velocity, makes this the principle on which the whole of mechanics depends, and does not mention the dispute.

confidence.printed: Upon this easy principle depends the whole of mechanics
